audio_lines.text: Christmas morning, 1914.
In a few seconds, this man will walk toward the German guns.
Unarmed. Across the ground where men had been dying for a few yards of mud.
That Christmas, thousands of soldiers on both sides did the same.
This is the day the war stopped, along parts of the Western Front. How it began, with a song. And how it ended.
The war had begun in August. Everyone said it would be over by Christmas.

audio_lines.delivery_direction: the line draws as he speaks
audio_lines.text: By December it had dug itself into the ground: one line of trenches, from the North Sea to Switzerland.
Here, in Flanders, the two sides sat close enough to hear each other cough.
Mud to the knee. Water in every boot. A sniper waiting for one careless head.
Private Thomas Hale had read the same line every night for a week.

audio_lines.delivery_direction: a tired half-smile, holding up the letter
audio_lines.text: Home by Christmas, she says. Didn't say which one.

audio_lines.delivery_direction: dry, not unkind, cleaning his rifle
audio_lines.text: Keep your head down, and you might see one.

audio_lines.delivery_direction: plain; a dry beat before the last sentence
audio_lines.text: In early December, the Pope asked for a Christmas truce. The appeal failed. No official truce was agreed. Nobody asked the men in the trenches.

audio_lines.delivery_direction: lighter, a small smile in the voice
audio_lines.text: At Christmas, parcels came up the line. British soldiers opened brass tins from Princess Mary: cigarettes, tobacco, a Christmas card.
On the German side, little Christmas trees had come up the line. As night fell, they went up on the parapets, candles and all.
Gefreiter Friedrich Brandt had carried this photograph since August.

audio_lines.delivery_direction: sung softly, a tenor line with men joining
audio_lines.text: Stille Nacht, heilige Nacht...
What are they singing?
Silent Night. Same tune as ours.

audio_lines.delivery_direction: flat, not looking away from the parapet
audio_lines.text: Let 'em sing. Heads down.
(Thomas does not answer; he looks at the candles)

audio_lines.delivery_direction: sung, unsure at first, then steadier
audio_lines.text: Silent night... holy night...
Good, English! More!
And for the first time in months, the sound crossing no man's land was not gunfire.
Christmas morning came white and still.
English! Merry Christmas!

audio_lines.delivery_direction: flat, a hand on his rifle
audio_lines.text: It's a trick. Nobody move.
No shooting! Merry Christmas!
(Thomas leans his rifle on the sandbags and climbs the ladder)
Thomas! Get back down!
If they wanted us dead, we'd be dead.
In places, the lines were only fifty yards apart. Fifty yards of frozen mud, wire, and the men who never made it back.
You are English?
And you're German?
(their empty hands)
Saxon. Fritz, to my friends. Merry Christmas, Tommy.
We're all Tommies to you. It's really my name.
(they shake hands)
Up and down this part of the line, the same thing was happening. Nobody had ordered it.
Along the British line in Flanders, it spread from trench to trench, in patches.
Nobody counted them. The usual estimate is that about a hundred thousand men took part.
They traded cigarettes, food, buttons. In a few places, accounts describe men kicking a ball around.
Where'd you learn English?

audio_lines.delivery_direction: a small proud smile, taking the cigarette
audio_lines.text: London. I was a waiter. Four years.
Many Germans had worked in Britain before the war. One Briton found his old barber among them, and sat down for a haircut.
You have a family?
My mum. And a little sister.
My wife. My daughter. She is three.
(Thomas looks at the photograph)
She looks happy.
She thinks I am home for Christmas.

audio_lines.delivery_direction: after a pause, barely above a breath
audio_lines.text: So does mine.
But the day was not only for trading. Both sides went out to bring in their dead.
Some had lain out there for weeks.
(two spades stand in the earth by the grave)
What was his name?

audio_lines.delivery_direction: the name steady; then he looks down
audio_lines.text: Karl. He sang the loudest.
I'm sorry.
At one burial, a Scottish chaplain read the Twenty-Third Psalm. A German student read it after him, in German.
(Harris takes off his cap at the edge of the graves)
By late afternoon, the light was going.
Tommy... why are we fighting?
I don't know.
They told us you were the enemy.
(Thomas looks at Friedrich)
They told us the same about you.
Tomorrow, maybe, we are enemies again.

audio_lines.delivery_direction: a beat after 'Maybe'; firm, warm on 'not today'
audio_lines.text: Maybe. But not today.
(Thomas cuts a brass button off his tunic with a penknife)
Something to remember me by.

audio_lines.delivery_direction: warm, a small smile, already twisting a button off
audio_lines.text: Then take one of mine.

audio_lines.delivery_direction: slow, warm, a held breath at the end
audio_lines.text: The sun went down on Christmas Day. Neither of them moved to leave.
The next morning, the men drifted back to their own trenches.
Good luck, Tommy.

audio_lines.delivery_direction: the nickname said warmly, a gift back
audio_lines.text: You too, Fritz.
Stand to.
At Houplines, on Boxing Day morning, a British captain ended it politely: shots into the air.
(the German captain salutes back, gets down into his trench, then fires two shots into the air)
(Thomas looks up at the shots)
There had been no treaty. In some places the truce lasted hours. In others, it held until the New Year.
Thomas wrote home that night. So did many others. In January, British newspapers printed their letters.
Their commanders moved to prevent it from happening again. A few small truces still occurred in 1915, but nothing on that scale.
The war went on for almost four more years.
(on screen: For one day, they remembered they were human.)
